newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Police sift evidence in hunt for Taiwan assassins.
newsitem.headline: Police sift evidence in hunt for Taiwan assassins.

text.p: Amid cries of public outrage, Taiwan police said on Friday they had solid evidence in the gangland-style execution of a county magistrate and seven others and vowed to apprehend the assassins swiftly.
"The most direct evidence is the fingerprints. We have collected quite a few," said National Police Administration director-general Yao Kao-chiao.
"Police have been working day and night to identify the fingerprints," Yao said. "Once we identify them, we will be able to solve the case."

Two gunmen burst into Taoyuan county magistrate Liu Pang-yu's home, bound the hands of Liu and eight others and methodically shot each in the head at close range on Thursday in one of Taiwan's most sensational crimes in memory.
Five died at the scene and Liu, 54, a member of the ruling Nationalist Party, and two others died at hospital.
Among the dead was another elected official, Taoyuan county councilman Chuang Shun-hsing. The only surviving victim, also an elected councilman, Teng Wen-chang, was in critical condition.
A Filipina maid who was in Liu's house during the shootings was under heavy police protection, as were Liu's widow and two people found bound but unharmed in the abandoned getaway car.
Police said the killers worked swiftly and that their actions had all the signs of a premeditated assassination.
"I have been a police officer for more than 30 years and I have not seen a case like this," said Wang Yi-fang, police chief of Taiwan's provincial government.

While officials condemned the killing, commentators and lawmakers expressed outrage and fear over the social chaos that has accompanied Taiwan's decade-old democratic renaissance and concern over some politicians close ties to organised crime.
"Taiwan has become the Republic of Crime," said opposition lawmaker Parris Chang, playing on Taiwan's official name, the Republic of China.
"Taiwan is not Sicily. It is more Sicilian than Sicily," lawmaker Yen Chin-fu said in one of a chorus of comparisons to Italy's Sicily-based mafia.
Liu was no stranger to suspicion. He was indicted on graft charges in August and was under investigation for illegal land speculation and even forgery of a masters degree.

The Justice Ministry in August launched a crackdown on scores of crime gangs that Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao said had infiltrated Taiwan's business and political circles and even parliament, triggering fears of underworld reprisals.
Local media have suspected the killings could involve a property development case.
